expectations.evidence: Turn 1 declines to affirm 'why they matter' and instead asks the visitor to specify what's threatened, redirecting to their own reasoning.
Turn 2 poses two competing formulations of the visitor's claim and asks which one they mean rather than settling it.
Turn 3 asks the visitor to name a concrete threshold rather than accepting or rejecting the 'threshold' framing itself.

Turn 4 states an interpretation of the visitor's own drift ('that's not even your argument anymore') but immediately converts it into a pressure test question about wicked vs tame problems, not a final verdict.
[held] Turn 2 introduces a genuinely new angle (hiding vs erasure distinction) and demands a concrete case, giving the visitor real material to work with.
[held] Turn 3 sharpens the challenge by demanding an observable threshold instead of repeating the prior objection verbatim.
[held] Turn 4 introduces the Rittel/Webber wicked-problem distinction to test whether 'failed the problem's constraints' even applies, a new substantive angle.
Turn 4 explicitly refuses to treat the visitor's sharper claim as settled, calling it a possible 'tame-problem move' imported into a wicked-problem context.
No turn narrates its own technique (e.g., no 'let me play devil's advocate' or 'as your sparring partner') — all challenges are delivered in-argument.

Turn 4 correctly invokes the Rittel/Webber definition of wicked problems (no stopping rule, no true/false test only better/worse relative to stakeholders) and applies it precisely to challenge the visitor's tame-problem-style threshold.
Each turn is short (1-3 tight paragraphs), opens directly with the sharpest counter-move, and avoids hedging language like 'perhaps' or 'it could be argued'.
